summary: In Greek mythology, Battus (Ancient Greek Βάττος) is the old herdsman who witnesses Hermes driving off Apollo's cattle. Bribed with a heifer to keep silence, he betrays the secret when Hermes returns in disguise and offers a richer reward; the god turns him to stone — the touchstone that tests gold. Ovid sets him by Neleus' pastures; handbook traditions also place the witness in Arcadia.
etymology: Ancient Greek Βάττος, traditionally "tongue-tied" or stammerer; the stone becomes the touchstone (basanos) that betrays false metal as Battus betrayed his oath.
cultCenters: Pieria / Neleus' pasture (Ovidian setting in the atlas)

sections.heading: Witness and perjury
paragraphs: On the day of his birth Hermes steals Apollo's herd. Only Battus sees the theft. Hermes leads him aside and promises a cow if he will keep silence; returning in another shape, the god offers a bull and a cow for news of the cattle, and the old man promptly betrays the secret. Hermes petrifies him — in Ovid, into the touchstone that reveals gold.

The atlas id battus-pieria follows the Pierian / Neleian pasture strand of the cattle theft. Wikipedia's short Battus stub stresses an Arcadian Maenalus setting in some handbooks; both are the same oath-breaking witness, not Battus of Cyrene the historical colonist.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: Do not confuse this mythic herdsman with Battus I of Cyrene or other historical bearers of the name.
